narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 55.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. First, your plan to attend part-time had the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. Among students who were accepted, only 7.2% planned to study part-time while 92.8% planned to attend full-time; the model sees part-time enrollment as a meaningful risk for first-time bar success.

Second, your LSAT score of 33.5 pulled the prediction in the opposite direction, toward passing. It was, however, lower than the average of 37.2 among accepted students, so it could not fully offset the other risks.

Third, your undergraduate GPA of 3.30 also favored passing and was actually slightly higher than the 3.23 average among accepted applicants. Unfortunately, this positive signal was not strong enough to overcome the part-time attendance factor.

In short, the combination of part-time study plans and a below-average LSAT score outweighed your solid grades and led the model to conclude your chance of passing the bar on the first try was too low for admission.

What you should do next is consider reapplying with a full-time study plan or retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Either change would directly address the two biggest concerns the model identified.
